# POWER ANAYLSIS --- RECOMMENDATIONS FOR MONITORING PROGRAM DESIGN/SAMPLING FREQUENCY

We chose a case study of the Hard Bottom Longline Hook Survey to evaluate sampling design requirements using power analysis to assess how monitoring programs could be adapted or expanded to detect meaningful changes in conservation priority species. 
Power analysis is a widely used approach for evaluating how sampling design and replication influence the ability to detect ecological change when it occurs. 
Statistical power depends on the magnitude of the effect being tested, the degree of spatial and temporal variability in indicators, and the level of replication across sites, years, and sampling units (Stewart-Oaten et al. 1986; Underwood 1994). 
In impact monitoring frameworks such as Before--After--Control--Impact (BACI) designs, balanced designs with comparable numbers of observations in pre- and post-impact periods generally provide greater statistical power than unbalanced designs with the same total sampling effort (Underwood 1994; Smokorowski and Randall 2017).

The Hard Bottom Longline Survey was selected as an illustrative example for several reasons. 
The HBLL was one of the programs that scored highest in our program assessment based on temporal suitability, domain relevance, and spatial coverage criteria. 
It has a 19-year time series providing sufficient historical data to characterize baseline variability, monitors multiple MPAN Ecological Conservation Priority rockfish species (yelloweye, quillback), samples 54 individual protected areas with coverage both inside and outside MPAN boundaries, and collects detailed biological data (length, weight, archived otoliths) enabling analysis of multiple response metrics.

The power analyses conducted on the HBLL were used to inform recommendations on sampling frequency, spatial replication, and temporal coverage needed to support robust evaluation of Marine Protected Area (MPA) performance.
Importantly, this case study serves as one methodological example---not a prescription. 
The HBLL was not originally designed for MPA performance assessment; sampling locations were selected for regional stock assessment. 
The power analysis demonstrates what is currently feasible with existing data and what adaptations would strengthen performance monitoring. 
Different programs will require different adaptations depending on their design, species monitored, spatial scale, logistical constraints, and organizational priorities.
This case study illustrates a general analytical workflow that can be applied to other high-suitability programs, with final decisions about program adaptation to be made collaboratively by Network Partners through the Network Monitoring Strategy process.

## MONITORING PROGRAM DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

*here we could have the section on sampling/monitoring program design stuff from the intro?*

**Statistical robustness in monitoring**

Effective sampling and monitoring design requires statistical robustness, incorporating careful consideration of sample size, replication, statistical power, and data independence. 
Neves et al. (In prep.) provides comprehensive discussion of factors involved in monitoring program sampling design, including various sample design
types, BACI approaches, and reference site selection (DFO 2021a).

**Replication**

Establishing appropriate replication levels---whether measured in number of sites, years, or samples within sites---presents significant challenges and varies considerably among projects and indicators (Braun et al. 2019). 
Power analyses serve as valuable tools for understanding how replication influences statistical power, defined as the ability to detect effects when they exist. 
Statistical power depends on several key factors: spatial and temporal variation in indicators, the strength of relationships between indicators and responses (effect size), and replication or sample size including number of sites, years, and plots.

Power analyses can employ standard methods for simple statistical analyses or utilize simulations for more complex modeling approaches (Johnson et al. 2015). 
These analyses require assumptions about spatial and temporal variability of indicators and effect sizes specific to individual studies and indicators.

**Temporal considerations and study design**

Increasing the number of years of data collection generally enhances statistical power. 
Balanced designs with equal numbers of before and after years provide greater statistical power than unbalanced designs using the same total number of years (Braun et al. 2019). 
O\'Neal et al. (2016) recommends collecting a minimum of two years of before-project data, matched with two years of after-project data. 
While acquiring pre-project data can be challenging, the statistical benefits of balanced design make a compelling case for investing in before-project data collection when feasible (Braun et al. 2019).

Within the NSB context, MPA sites experiencing greater pre-implementation fishing intensity and other pressures may demonstrate higher power to detect management-related changes compared to sites with historically lower human activity levels.

**Before-After-Control-Impact (BACI) design**

BACI design represents one of the most appropriate methods for evaluating management measure performance. 
This approach proves particularly powerful because it controls for both temporal and spatial variation, thereby improving the robustness of conclusions regarding management effects. 
BACI design compares sampling periods before and after measure implementation alongside impacted and control sites.

Successful BACI implementation requires suitable reference sites (control sites) that remain fixed throughout the study period, while within-site sampling units may be re-randomized or maintained as fixed locations. 
External reference sites are highly recommended to optimize conclusion scope and are required for BACI or similar sampling designs. 
These sites should be positioned sufficiently distant from protected areas to avoid edge effects, maintain comparable environmental conditions and substrates, and exhibit similar historical pressure
levels (DFO 2021a).

**Reference sites and monitoring**

Areas currently under monitoring outside protected areas serve as invaluable reference sites for assessing MPA performance and impact. 
These monitored zones, often sharing similar ecological characteristics with MPA areas, provide comparative benchmarks for evaluating changes and patterns within protected regions (Nature United 2023). 
Through examination of these external areas, scientists and conservationists can establish meaningful parallels, contrasting impacts of human activities and environmental changes in unprotected regions against conservation outcomes within MPAs.

Reference areas facilitate understanding of natural variations, human-induced pressures, and potential benefits derived from protective measures. 
Analysis of differences and similarities enables assessment of MPA efficacy, providing critical information for adaptive management and conservation strategy refinement within protected marine environments.

Reference monitoring represents an emerging opportunity that utilizes well-managed MPA sites as reference points for understanding global and regional driver effects on ocean conditions (Fairweather 2012a; Fairweather 2012b). 
Since reference sites will develop over time, this approach has been identified as a low priority for the Network monitoring framework, strategy, and associated plans (Network Monitoring Framework). 
However, reference monitoring should be considered in subsequent iterations of Network monitoring following sufficient duration of site and Network establishment.

## POWER ANALYSIS METHODOLOGY

Since 2003, Fisheries and Oceans Canada has conducted Hard Bottom Longline (HBLL) surveys to monitor groundfish abundance and distribution off the coast of BC. 
The survey targets inshore rockfish habitat, specifically Yelloweye and Quillback rockfish habitat [@doherty2019]. 
The HBLL survey consists of two survey series: inside (HBLL INS, referring to waters between Vancouver Island and the mainland) and the outside (HBLL OUT, all other BC waters). 
North and south areas within each series are surveyed biennially. 
Three of the four regions (HBLL OUT N, HBLL OUT S, and HBLL INS N) overlap with the GBS MPA Network (Figure hbll-mpa-historical-overlay). 
The surveys use a depth-stratified random sampling design, with a target allocation of 189 sets (HBLL OUT N), 252 (HBLL OUT S), and 70 (HBLL INS N).

We used a simulation-based power analysis to assess the ability of existing monitoring programs to detect changes in population indices of groundfish across the MPA Network. 
Our approach consisted of four steps: (1) fit conditioning models to empirical data, (2) simulate population recovery trends inside and outside of the MPAs under the assumption of fishing cessation within MPAs, (3) apply two different sampling strategies to the simulated population, and (4) test the power of these sampling strategies to detect trends across the MPA Network by fitting another spatiotemporal model to the combined historical and simulated data.

Using a spatiotemporal modelling approach, we applied this power analysis to five conservation priority species that are well sampled by the HBLL survey: Yelloweye Rockfish, Quillback Rockfish, Lingcod, Pacific Halibut, and Pacific Spiny Dogfish. 
This approach allows us to test different scenarios, such as recovery trends within the MPA or evaluation time frame, while incorporating some ecological complexity and variability (Table \@ref(tab:scenario-summary)). 
Power increases with larger MPA effect sizes (e.g., faster recovery), higher abundances, wider spatial distribution, more frequent sampling, and longer evaluation times. 
Conversely, species with slower recovery rates, patchy distributions, and/or lower abundance will require more intensive sampling and longer evaluation time frames to detect population changes.

```

### Step 1: Fitting conditioning models

For each of the three HBLL survey regions and each species, we fit separate spatiotemporal models with the sdmTMB R package [@sdmTMB] of the form:

\begin{align}
  y_{\mathbf{s},t} &\sim \text{BetaBinomial}(n_{\mathbf{s},t}, \mu_{\mathbf{s},t}, \phi) \\
  \mu_{\mathbf{s},t} &= g^{-1}(\beta_t + \omega_\mathbf{s} + \epsilon_{\mathbf{s},t}) \\
  \omega_\mathbf{s} &\sim \text{MVNormal}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_\omega^{-1}) \\
  \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{t} &\sim \text{MVNormal}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{Q}_\epsilon^{-1})
\end{align}

We modelled the number of hooks catching a given species $y_{\mathbf{s},t}$ at each location $\mathbf{s}$ and year $t$.
We used a beta-binomial observation model, which is a generalization of the binomial distribution in which the probability of success is not fixed but varies according to a beta distribution.
This allows the model to capture additional variance across trials compared to the binomial distribution.
The symbol $n_{\mathbf{s},t}$ is the number of ``trials'' (here the number of hooks in a given survey set),
$\mu_{\mathbf{s},t}$ is the expected probability of a hook catching a fish, and
$\phi$ is the dispersion parameter where smaller values of $\phi$ result in greater variance: $\mathrm{Var}(y) = n\mu(1-\mu)\frac{n+\phi}{1+\phi}$.
The function $g^{-1}$ represents the (inverse) complementary log-log ("cloglog") link chosen for its connection to the Poisson sampling process and its use in integrated data modelling.

The beta-binomial distribution was the most parsimonious probability distribution when compared using AIC against Poisson and negative binomial models fitted with fish counts as the response and log hook count as an offset.
Importantly, the beta-binomial constrained the number of fish observed to be within the number of hooks set and therefore produced simulated data that more closely resembled the observed data.
See supplementary materials for model comparison of hook and line count data simulation diagnostics.
    
Our linear predictor included an annual mean fixed effect ($\beta_t$) and 
spatial ($\omega_\mathbf{s}$) and spatiotemporal ($\epsilon_{\mathbf{s},t}$) random effects. 
These random effects were structured as Gaussian Markov random fields (GMRFs) that were mean zero with precision matrices ($\mathbf{Q}_\omega$ and $\mathbf{Q}_\epsilon$; inverse covariance matrices) based on a Matérn spatial correlation function.
The spatial random fields account for constant spatial patterning or correlation in distribution while the spatiotemporal random fields account for spatial patterning that is unique each year.
If models failed to converge or if spatial and/or spatiotemporal variance estimates collapsed to near zero ($<$ 0.01), the models were refit with the collapsed random fields set to zero.
Models were considered to have converged if the Hessian matrix was positive definite and the absolute gradient of the marginal log-likelihood with respect to each fixed effect was $<$ 0.001.

TO FILL IN:

We did not account for hook competition.

Fit conditioning models for each of the three HBLL survey regions to maximize the ability for the simulated data to resemble the observed data.

Figure \@ref(fig:spp-distribution) shows the average spatial distribution from the fitted models for each species.

### Step 2: Simulate data from conditioning models

Dimensions included here: species, mpa effect (recovery rates from No Fishing scenarios Table \@ref(tab:recovery-rates), addition of spatiotemporal noise to increase realism.

Output: known truth, example of simulated time series shown in Figure \@ref(fig:historical-simulated-index-example).
Full grid for each species of values (possible additional figure -- or in supplement)

```{r recovery-rates}
rates <- readRDS(here::here("data-generated", "recovery-rates-lambda.rds"))
spp_levels <- rates |> arrange(lambda) |> pull(species) |> unique()

rates_table <- rates |>
  select(species, case, time, lambda, source, citekey) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = spp_levels)) |>
  mutate(
    species = forcats::fct_recode(species, "pacific spiny dogfish" = "north pacific spiny dogfish"),
    case = gsub("_", " ", case),
    case = gsub("median", "base", case),
    time = round(time),
    lambda = round(lambda, 3),
    percent_rate = 100 * (lambda - 1)
  ) |>
  select(species, case, time, `annual percent change` = percent_rate, citekey, source) |>
  arrange(species, `annual percent change`)

rates_table |>
  select(-time) |>
  rename(Species = species, Case = case, `Annual % change` = `annual percent change`, Citation = citekey, Source = source) |> 
  flextable() |>
  set_table_properties(layout = "autofit") |> 
  set_caption("Annual rates of change used in simulation of population recovery. Values derived from most recent stock assessment projections of no fishing scenarios.")
```

## POWER ANALYSIS RESULTS

Statistical power to detect MPA recovery trends varied across species and effect sizes.
For species with faster recovery rates, ≥80% power could be reached within the first 10--15 years of MPA implementation using status quo sampling, while for species with slower recovery it may take 20--25 years of monitoring.
Reducing MPA sampling frequency generally delayed when ≥80% power was reached.

Helps us set expectations:

- At best expect detection of MPA effects in the best sampled species within 10-15 years

- Rates of recovery \~ 1% per year expect to detect effects in 20-25 years

- Rates of recovery 2-3 % expect 10-15 years

- Rates \>4% expect within \<10 years

- Decreasing sampling within MPAs to every 4 years increased the number of years before we could detect an effect by \~ 5-10 years for a given recovery rate

Detection of significant effects before 10 years is likely to lead to over estimates of effects 🡪 high exaggeration rates.

Stock assessment "no fishing" scenarios and life histories can help to inform expectations of recovery rates
